Jim stood in the center of the advanced yoga studio, his face a mask of determination and impending doom. He was attempting the "Eagle Pose," but his legs were tangled like a pair of socks in a dryer, and his arms were crossed so tightly he looked like a mummy trying to hug itself.

The instructor, a serene woman named Serenity who hadn’t blinked in forty-five minutes, glided over. "Jim," she whispered, her voice like wind chimes in a gentle breeze. "You are holding your breath. And your dignity. Let it go."

"I can't," Jim grunted, his face turning a shade of purple usually reserved for bruised plums. "If I let go, I fall. If I fall, I break. If I break, I can't pay rent."

Just then, a low, resonant rumble echoed through the silent room. It wasn't the wind. It wasn't the building settling. It was Jim’s stomach, or perhaps his lower intestine, deciding to join the symphony. The class, previously frozen in perfect stillness, twitched. A woman in the back row opened one eye.

"Focus on your breath, Jim," Serenity said, though her left eye was now twitching in sympathy.

Jim tried to inhale, but the pressure in his abdomen was too great. He shifted his weight, trying to find a center of gravity that no longer existed. As he did, a sound escaped him—not a grunt this time, but a high-pitched squeak, like a rubber duck being stepped on by an elephant.

The class gasped. Not in horror, but in shared human vulnerability.

Then, the real trouble started. Jim, in his panic to stabilize himself, grabbed the shoulder of the person next to him. It was a large man named Dave, who was currently balancing on one leg in a pose that required the core strength of a steel beam. Dave wobbled. Jim wobbled. They both wobbled.

And then, from the back of the room, a long, mournful honk echoed.

Everyone turned. Standing in the doorway, looking utterly out of place in a suit and tie, was a giraffe.
